extracted.intended_audience: authors, poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in standards of poetry and literary reputation
extracted.subtask_description: Critical standards for assessing poetry and the ethics/practices of literary publication and promotion; includes guidance on poetic technique (imagery, simile, syntax, personification, unity) and on commercial/political practices (puffing, publicity, critic responsibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to puffing / artificial promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is high time to make a stand against the new trickery. The puffing of books is now so shamefully and so successfully carried on that it is the duty of all who are anxious for the purity of the national taste, or for the honour of the literary character, to join in discountenancing the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: employing journalists, placard-bearers, collusive notices, paid praises, or any artifice to 'stun the public' with praise. Authors and literary men should refuse to take part in or benefit from such contrivances; works should be recommended by their own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works should be recommended by their own merits (allow free criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is his business to take such precautions as may prevent others from doing what must degrade him. It is for his honour as a gentleman ... that his works should come before the public recommended by their own merits alone, and should be discussed with perfect freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should accept and invite genuine criticism rather than manufacture praise. The long-term interest of a writer of real talent is served by exposing work to free critical judgment rather than artificial puffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plagiarism and clumsy borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: A very amusing instance of literary pilfering ... what they steal is, to employ a phrase common in advertisements, of no use to any but the right owner. We never fell in, however, with any plunderer who so little understood how to turn his booty to good account as Mr. Montgomery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: near-verbatim appropriations of Byron, Campbell, Scott, Dryden. Anti-patterns: lifting images without understanding or adapting them; borrowed lines that make no sense out of their original context. Plagiarism not only unethical but typically yields poor results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness and logical fitness of similes and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: We take this to be, on the whole, the worst similitude in the world. In the first place, no stream meanders, or can possibly meander, level with its fount. In the next place, if streams did meander level with their founts, no two motions can be less like each other than that of meandering level and that of mounting upwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similes must have clear, observable analogies and be contextually appropriate. Anti-patterns: comparisons that are self-contradictory, physically impossible, or bear no real resemblance to the thing compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual appropriateness of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison of a violet, bright with the dew, to a woman’s eyes, is as perfect as a comparison can be. Sir Walter’s lines are part of a song addressed to a woman at daybreak... Dew on a bramble is no more like a woman’s eyes than dew anywhere else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the imagery fits the scene, situation, or speaker. Borrowed or recycled images can be grotesque if taken out of their original context; choose images that naturally suit the poem's circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct syntax and clear grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Robert Montgomery’s readers must take such grammar as they can get ... We should be glad to know what the word 'For' means here. If it is a preposition, it makes nonsense of the words, 'Thy mercy tempers.' If it is an adverb, it makes nonsense of the words, 'Thy cares provide.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammatical errors and syntactic confusion undercut meaning and dignity. Authors should ensure clauses, pronouns, and function words work together to produce sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of incoherent or nonsensical phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: No field-preacher surely ever carried his irreverent familiarity so far as to bid the Supreme Being stop and think on the importance of the interests which are under His care. The grotesque indecency of such an address throws into shade the subordinate absurdities of the passage...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases that produce unintended or absurd meanings (e.g., telling God to 'pause and think') are failures of diction/tone. Revise to remove grotesque or unintentionally irreverent turns of phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and unity of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The second part is a series of descriptions of various events ... Mr. Robert Montgomery terminates each of these descriptions by assuring us that the Deity was present at the battle, murder, execution, marriage or funeral in question. And this proposition ... forms the only link which connects these descriptions with the subject or with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each section or episode should relate meaningfully to the central subject; avoid episodic lists joined only by a repetitious slogan. Structural links must be substantive, not merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty bombast, mixed metaphors, and inflated grandiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: This patchwork, made by stitching together old odds and ends of what, when new, was but tawdry frippery, is to be picked off the dunghill ... A roaring cataract of nonsense is poured forth upon this tremendous subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grand statements and sublime language must be founded on genuine insight and precise imagery. Resist piling up unrelated 'sublime' phrases or extravagant metaphors that produce noise rather than meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense and semantic precision in diction
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Dropp’d' is false English. 'Thy look obedience' means the very reverse of what Mr. Robert Montgomery intends to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words that convey the intended meaning; test unusual constructions to ensure they communicate rather than invert sense. Avoid archaisms or contractions that distort sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification must be meaningful and defensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Robert Montgomery is fond of personification, and belongs ... to that school of poets who hold that nothing more is necessary to a personification in poetry than to begin a word with a capital letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personifications should illuminate rather than confuse: give them motivations or relations that make allegorical figures intelligible. Anti-patterns: arbitrary capitalization or personification without clear semantic role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency in argument and metaphor across the work
rubrics_metrics.description: He informs us that lightning is designless and self-created. If he can believe this, we cannot conceive why he may not believe that the whole universe is designless and self-created. A few lines before, he tells us that it is the Deity who bids 'thunder rattle from the skiey deep.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent premises and imagery; avoid asserting mutually contradictory claims in adjacent passages. Check that theological, philosophical, or causal claims cohere throughout the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of meaning — avoid garbled or opaque conceits
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the meaning of the two lines which almost immediately follow? 'A soulless thing, a spirit of the woods, / He loves to commune with the fields and floods.' How can a soulless thing be a spirit?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metaphors and descriptions are intelligible. If an image requires paradox, make the paradox rhetorically evident; do not produce plain contradiction or meaningless combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity over contrived sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: We can, however, conscientiously declare that persons of the most excitable sensibility may safely venture upon Mr. Robert Montgomery’s version [of a Crabbe passage].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genuine emotional effect arises from apt detail and truthful depiction; avoid manufacturing sentiment by crude or exaggerated language that fails to move a perceptive reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on journals/critics to manufacture reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher plays Buckingham to the author’s Richard ... The rabble at first stare and wonder, and at last join in shouting for shouting’s sake; and thus a crown is placed on a head which has no right to it, by the huzzas of a few servile dependants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not depend on orchestrated press campaigns or collusive reviews to establish literary worth. Reputation built on such noise blocks access for genuinely meritorious writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of critics: expose nonsense rather than be lenient
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are best fitted to guide the public opinion think it beneath them to expose mere nonsense, and comfort themselves by reflecting that such popularity cannot last. This contemptuous lenity has been carried too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent critics should point out errors and bad art rather than ignore them on grounds of decorum. Failure to criticize allows low-quality work to proliferate and mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between form and subject (tone/suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: No field-preacher surely ever carried his irreverent familiarity so far as to bid the Supreme Being stop and think on the importance of the interests which are under His care. The grotesque indecency of such an address throws into shade the subordinate absurdities of the passage...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone and register to the subject matter: solemn subjects demand measured handling; levity or familiarity can become indecent when mismatched to theme or object of address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in allegory and ordering of allegorical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the distinction between the foul orgies and the raging havoc which the foul orgies are to picture? Why does Fright go behind Rebellion, and Murder before?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using allegory, ensure the placement and relations of personified abstractions make rhetorical sense. The order and roles of allegorical attendants must have a defensible logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid patchwork composition and over-reliance on stock phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: This patchwork, made by stitching together old odds and ends of what, when new, was but tawdry frippery, is to be picked off the dunghill on which it ought to rot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality of thought and phrasing is preferable to assembling clichés and well-worn epithets. Recycled 'stock' effects produce an immediate sense of cheapness and artlessness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure images and actions are physically and logically possible
rubrics_metrics.description: We take this to be, on the whole, the worst similitude in the world. In the first place, no stream meanders, or can possibly meander, level with its fount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test images against real-world plausibility to avoid absurd comparisons. Impossible or self-contradictory images undermine credibility and poetic effect.
